\chapter{Completing the Preterite --- Three Families, One Question}
\label{ch:completing-preterite}
\hlchaptermodality{39}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can form the singular completed past of regular -er/-ir verbs and the known strong verbs tener, hacer, and estar.}

Complete ES-C15-practice and retrieve the bounded singular sets for comer, vivir, tener, hacer, and estar with their spelling and historical contrasts.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[comí]{comí — one regular -er singular past}

\label{lesson:ES-C15-comer-preterite}



\begin{quote}
You know present \textbf{como, comes, come} and the singular \textbf{-ar} past. To make a completed past from \textbf{comer}, keep \textbf{com-} and learn three forms: \textbf{comí, comiste, comió}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: present beside completed past}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{present} & \textbf{completed past} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{como} & \textbf{comí} \\
tú & \textbf{comes} & \textbf{comiste} \\
él / ella / usted & \textbf{come} & \textbf{comió} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say \textbf{comí · comiste · comió}. Keep the limit visible: these are the same three familiar singular persons. Plural forms wait.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: final stress in two forms}]
\textbf{Comí} and \textbf{comió} carry written accents because their stress falls on the final vowel. \textbf{Comiste} follows ordinary next-to-last stress, so it needs no mark. The three forms by themselves make complete utterances:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Comí.} — “I ate.”
  \item \textbf{¿Comiste?} — “Did you eat?”
  \item \textbf{Comió.} — “He, she, or you-formal ate.”
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Spanish \textbf{comer} continues Latin \textbf{comedere}. Its regular past endings also continue Latin perfect material, including forms with \textbf{-ī, -istī, -it}. Sound change and analogy reshaped that material across Romance into Spanish \textbf{-í, -iste, -ió}. The resemblance is real, but it is not one tidy chain in which every modern ending merely drops a letter.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “comí, comiste, comió”
  \item “Como. Comí.”
  \item “comí and comió carry final-stress accents”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the three learned \textbf{comer} forms. (\emph{Comí, comiste, comió.}) Which carry written accents? (\emph{Comí} and \emph{comió}.) What shaped the modern endings? (Latin perfect material, sound change, and analogy.) Next: reuse the same endings with a known \textbf{-ir} verb.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[viví]{viví — reuse one past pattern with an -ir verb}

\label{lesson:ES-C15-comer-vivir-preterite}



\begin{quote}
You know present \textbf{vivo, vives, vive}, and you just learned past \textbf{comí, comiste, comió}. Keep \textbf{viv-} and reuse those three past endings: \textbf{viví, viviste, vivió}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one -ir singular past}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{present} & \textbf{completed past} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{vivo} & \textbf{viví} \\
tú & \textbf{vives} & \textbf{viviste} \\
él / ella / usted & \textbf{vive} & \textbf{vivió} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say \textbf{viví · viviste · vivió}. Reuse known \textbf{en} for a small contrast:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Vivo en Madrid.} — “I live in Madrid.”
  \item \textbf{Viví en Madrid.} — “I lived in Madrid.”
  \item \textbf{¿Viviste en Madrid?} — “Did you live in Madrid?”
  \item \textbf{Vivió en Madrid.} — “He, she, or you-formal lived in Madrid.”
\end{itemize}

The written accents in \textbf{viví} and \textbf{vivió} show final stress. \textbf{Viviste} already has ordinary next-to-last stress and needs no mark.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: -er and -ir meet in this past}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{\textbf{comer}} & \textbf{\textbf{vivir}} \\
\midrule
yo & com\textbf{í} & viv\textbf{í} \\
tú & com\textbf{iste} & viv\textbf{iste} \\
él / ella / usted & com\textbf{ió} & viv\textbf{ió} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The shared endings are \textbf{-í} in the first row, \textbf{-iste} in the second, and \textbf{-ió} in the third. The presents differ, but these two singular past rows converge on one ending set. That is a fact about the forms you have learned, not permission to guess plural forms; those wait.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Spanish \textbf{vivir} continues Latin \textbf{vīvere}. Its modern past endings belong to the same Romance history as the \textbf{comer} endings: Latin perfect material was reshaped by sound change and analogy. The shared \textbf{-iste} is a useful family resemblance, not proof of one simple letter-by-letter erosion.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “viví, viviste, vivió”
  \item “Vivo en Madrid. Viví en Madrid.”
  \item “comí and viví share -í; comió and vivió share -ió”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the three learned \textbf{vivir} forms. (\emph{Viví, viviste, vivió.}) Which past endings do \textbf{comer} and \textbf{vivir} share? (\emph{-í, -iste, -ió.}) Which two carry written accents? (\emph{Viví} and \emph{vivió}.) Next, keep the singular limit but let the stem change.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tuve]{tuve — let the strong stem carry the stress}

\label{lesson:ES-C15-tener-preterite}



\begin{quote}
You know present \textbf{tengo, tienes, tiene}. Its completed past changes the stem to \textbf{tuv-} and uses \textbf{tuve, tuviste, tuvo}. Unlike \textbf{comí} and \textbf{comió}, none of these three forms carries a written accent.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one strong singular pattern}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{present} & \textbf{completed past} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{tengo} & \textbf{tuve} \\
tú & \textbf{tienes} & \textbf{tuviste} \\
él / ella / usted & \textbf{tiene} & \textbf{tuvo} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The strong stem \textbf{tuv-} takes \textbf{-e, -iste, -o}. Say \textbf{tuve · tuviste · tuvo}. Stress remains in the stem, so normal spelling needs no accent mark. Reuse known \textbf{café}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Tuve café.} — “I had coffee.”
  \item \textbf{¿Tuviste café?} — “Did you have coffee?”
  \item \textbf{Tuvo café.} — “He, she, or you-formal had coffee.”
\end{itemize}

“Strong” describes the stem-stressed historical pattern. It does not mean that the meaning is forceful. Plural endings wait.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Tener} continues Latin \textbf{tenēre}. Its past also belongs to an older strong history associated with Latin \textbf{tenuī}. Spanish sound change and analogy reshaped that material into the \textbf{tuv-} family. \textbf{Tenuī $\to$ tuve} is therefore a historical relationship, not a promise that every letter passed across intact.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “tuve, tuviste, tuvo”
  \item “Tuve café.”
  \item “comí has final stress; tuve has stem stress”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the three learned \textbf{tener} forms. (\emph{Tuve, tuviste, tuvo.}) Which endings attach to \textbf{tuv-}? (\emph{-e, -iste, -o.}) Why are there no written accents? (The strong stem carries the stress.) What shaped \textbf{tuve} historically? (Older strong-perfect material, sound change, and analogy.) Next: reuse the strong endings with \textbf{hacer}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hice]{hice — the strong pattern with one third-person swerve}

\label{lesson:ES-C15-hacer-preterite}



\begin{quote}
You know present \textbf{hago, haces, hace} and strong past \textbf{tuve, tuviste, tuvo}. \textbf{Hacer} reuses the strong endings: \textbf{hice, hiciste, hizo}. Watch the third form: the stem is \textbf{hiz-} there, not \textbf{hic-}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: hacer in the completed past}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{completed past} & \textbf{stem plus ending} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{hice} & \textbf{hic- + -e} \\
tú & \textbf{hiciste} & \textbf{hic- + -iste} \\
él / ella / usted & \textbf{hizo} & \textbf{hiz- + -o} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say \textbf{hice · hiciste · hizo}. These are strong, stem-stressed forms with no written accents. \textbf{Hizo} is an irregular stem alternation inside this family; it is not a general rule that \textbf{c} must become \textbf{z} before \textbf{o}. Reuse known \textbf{café}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Hice café.} — “I made coffee.”
  \item \textbf{¿Hiciste café?} — “Did you make coffee?”
  \item \textbf{Hizo café.} — “He, she, or you-formal made coffee.”
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Hacer} continues Latin \textbf{facere}, and \textbf{hice} continues the history of its strong perfect \textbf{fēcī}. Long sound changes help explain Spanish \textbf{h-} and the changed vowel and consonant; this is not a direct spelling recipe. The pattern links \textbf{hice} historically to strong \textbf{tuve}, while each verb keeps its own stem.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “hice, hiciste, hizo”
  \item “Hice café.”
  \item “hizo is a learned hiz- alternation, not a general c-before-o rule”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the three learned \textbf{hacer} forms. (\emph{Hice, hiciste, hizo.}) What changes in the third form? (\textbf{Hic-} becomes \textbf{hiz-}.) Is that a general \textbf{c-before-o} spelling rule? (No; learn it inside this irregular family.) What older form lies behind \textbf{hice}? (Latin \textbf{fēcī}, through substantial historical change.) Next: add strong \textbf{estar} without adding plural forms.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[estuve]{estuve — a third known verb joins the strong pattern}

\label{lesson:ES-C15-preterite-fuertes}



\begin{quote}
You know present \textbf{estoy, estás, está} and the strong past pairs \textbf{tuve, tuviste, tuvo} and \textbf{hice, hiciste, hizo}. Now use the same strong endings with \textbf{estuv-}: \textbf{estuve, estuviste, estuvo}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: estar in the completed past}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{completed past} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{estuve} \\
tú & \textbf{estuviste} \\
él / ella / usted & \textbf{estuvo} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say \textbf{estuve · estuviste · estuvo}. The strong stem \textbf{estuv-} takes \textbf{-e, -iste, -o}. These forms carry no written accents. Reuse known \textbf{bien}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Estuve bien.} — “I was well.”
  \item \textbf{¿Estuviste bien?} — “Were you well?”
  \item \textbf{Estuvo bien.} — “He, she, or you-formal was well.”
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three strong singular rows}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item yo: \textbf{tuve · hice · estuve}.
  \item tú: \textbf{tuviste · hiciste · estuviste}.
  \item él / ella / usted: \textbf{tuvo · hizo · estuvo}.
\end{itemize}

All three rows use the learned strong endings. Only \textbf{hacer} changes its stem shape from \textbf{hic-} to \textbf{hiz-} before third-person \textbf{-o}. Plural forms and other irregular verbs still wait.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Estar} grew from a Romance verb related to Latin \textbf{stāre}, “stand.” But modern \textbf{estuve} is not a direct, tidy wearing-down of Latin \textbf{stetī}. Historical analogy helped reshape its past beside other strong forms, including the \textbf{-uv-} pattern visible in \textbf{tuve}. This explains the family resemblance without pretending that each modern letter came straight from one Latin form.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “estuve, estuviste, estuvo”
  \item “Estuve bien.”
  \item “tuve and estuve share -uv- through historical analogy”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the three learned \textbf{estar} forms. (\emph{Estuve, estuviste, estuvo.}) Which known strong verb shares their \textbf{-uv-} shape? (\emph{Tener: tuve.}) Why should \textbf{estuve} not be shown as a direct wearing-down of \textbf{stetī}? (Analogy reshaped the Spanish family.) Next: retrieve all six bounded patterns.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — six singular patterns, no hidden vocabulary}

\label{lesson:ES-C15-practice}



\begin{quote}
This checkpoint adds nothing. Retrieve only the three singular persons of each learned row. Every word in the short sentences is already known.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the complete frame for this chapter}]
Regular rows:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{yo:} \textbf{hablé · comí · viví}.
  \item \textbf{tú:} \textbf{hablaste · comiste · viviste}.
  \item \textbf{él / ella / usted:} \textbf{habló · comió · vivió}.
\end{itemize}

Strong rows:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{yo:} \textbf{tuve · hice · estuve}.
  \item \textbf{tú:} \textbf{tuviste · hiciste · estuviste}.
  \item \textbf{él / ella / usted:} \textbf{tuvo · hizo · estuvo}.
\end{itemize}

The \textbf{-er} and \textbf{-ir} rows share \textbf{-í, -iste, -ió}. The three strong rows share \textbf{-e, -iste, -o}, but their stems must be learned: \textbf{tuv-, hic-/hiz-, estuv-}. Plural persons, more strong verbs, and new time or setting vocabulary remain outside this checkpoint.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: let spelling show the stress}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Regular \textbf{comí, comió, viví, vivió} carry written accents for final stress.
  \item Strong \textbf{tuve, tuvo, hice, hizo, estuve, estuvo} carry no written accents; stress remains in the strong stem.
  \item \textbf{Comiste} and \textbf{viviste} need no accent because their ordinary stress is already next to last.
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
The regular \textbf{-er/-ir} endings continue Latin perfect material reshaped across Romance. \textbf{Tuve} and \textbf{hice} continue older strong-perfect histories, also reshaped rather than copied letter for letter. \textbf{Estuve} shows especially clear analogical remodeling beside the \textbf{-uv-} family of \textbf{tuve}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “hablé, comí, viví”
  \item “tuve, hice, estuve”
  \item “Hice café. Viví en Madrid. Estuve bien.”
  \item “comí and comió have accents; tuve and tuvo do not”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the regular \textbf{comer} and \textbf{vivir} sets. (\emph{Comí, comiste, comió; viví, viviste, vivió.}) Give the three strong sets. (\emph{Tuve, tuviste, tuvo; hice, hiciste, hizo; estuve, estuviste, estuvo.}) Which rows share endings? (\textbf{-er/-ir} share one regular set; the strong rows share another.) The next chapter can add a new past contrast without borrowing any plural form here.
\end{tcolorbox}
